title: Lifting The Maximally-entangledness Assumption In Robust Self-testing For Synchronous Games
authors: Matthijs Vernooij And Yuming Zhao
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2222 (2026).

Robust self-testing in non-local games allows a classical referee to certify that two untrustworthy players are able to perform a specific quantum strategy up to high precision. Proving robust self-testing results becomes significantly easier when one restricts the allowed strategies to symmetric projective maximally entangled (PME) strategies, which allow natural descriptions in terms of tracial von Neumann algebras. This has been exploited in the celebrated [MATH] paper and related articles to prove robust self-testing results for synchronous games when restricting to PME strategies. However, the PME assumptions are not physical, so these results need to be upgraded to make them physically relevant. In this work, we do just that: we prove that any perfect synchronous game which is a robust self-test when restricted to PME strategies, is in fact a robust self-test for all strategies. We then apply our result to the Quantum Low Degree Test to find an efficient [MATH]-qubit test.

.
tldr: The paper removes the nonphysical maximally entangled symmetric projective assumption from robust self-testing results for synchronous games, showing that PME self-tests imply full robust self-tests and applying this to the Quantum Low Degree Test.
motivation: Robust self-testing is central to device-independent certification, but many strong results for synchronous games have relied on symmetric projective maximally entangled (PME) strategies that are not physically justified.
method: The authors prove a lifting theorem: any perfect synchronous game that robustly self-tests against PME strategies also robustly self-tests against all strategies, using tracial von Neumann algebra techniques.
result: The lifting theorem is applied to the Quantum Low Degree Test, yielding an efficient qubit test without the PME assumption.
conclusion: This work upgrades PME-restricted robust self-testing results to physically relevant full robust self-testing, strengthening device-independent certification for synchronous games and the Quantum Low Degree Test.

title: Reliable Entropy Estimation From Observed Statistics For Device-Independent Quantum Cryptography
authors: Gereon Koßmann And René Schwonnek
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2238 (2026).

We introduce a numerical framework for reliably estimating conditional von Neumann entropies, a central quantity in device-independent quantum cryptography and randomness generation. Our method is based on semidefinite relaxations derived from the Navascués--Pironio--Acín hierarchy and provides entropy bounds directly from observed statistics, assuming only the validity of quantum mechanics. The approach builds on a recent integral representation of entropy and substantially improves efficiency: it requires about half as many support variables as existing methods, while allowing these variables to be chosen projectively, leading to a significant reduction in runtime. These advances enable the practical certification of randomness and security even in noisy conditions, while integrating seamlessly with modern entropy accumulation theorems. Consequently, our framework becomes a versatile tool for quantum cryptographic protocols, broadening the possibilities for secure communication in untrusted environments.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a numerical framework for reliably estimating conditional von Neumann entropies from observed statistics in device-independent quantum cryptography using semidefinite relaxations.
motivation: Device-independent cryptography and randomness generation require rigorous entropy bounds from observed data under minimal assumptions, but existing numerical methods can be computationally costly.
method: The authors build on the Navascués-Pironio-Acín hierarchy and a recent integral representation of entropy to construct semidefinite relaxations that yield entropy bounds directly from observed statistics.
result: The framework requires roughly half as many support variables as existing methods, allows projective variable choices, and significantly reduces runtime while remaining compatible with entropy accumulation theorems.
conclusion: This makes practical certification of randomness and security more efficient in noisy, untrusted-device settings and provides a versatile tool for quantum cryptographic protocols.

title: Self-testing Of Logical Subspaces Of Quantum Error-correcting Codes
authors: Li-Yi Hsu And En-Jui Kuo
abstract: We develop explicit device-independent self-testing constructions for logical subspaces of quantum error-correcting codes. By constructing multipartite Bell inequalities tailored to stabilizer code structures, we show that maximal quantum violations uniquely certify that the underlying shared state resides within the logical subspace of a given code, up to local isometries. These constructions extend earlier stabilizer-subspace self-testing results beyond the five-qubit code to several representative stabilizer codes, including the six-qubit code, the Steane code, and Shor’s nine-qubit code. The tilted sum-of-squares variants further impose algebraic constraints on the relative weights of the logical sectors. Together, these results provide explicit examples of device-independent self-testing for representative stabilizer-code logical subspaces and suggest possible directions for verification and benchmarking of encoded quantum information.
tldr: The paper develops explicit device-independent self-testing constructions for logical subspaces of several stabilizer quantum error-correcting codes using tailored multipartite Bell inequalities.
motivation: Self-testing is a central device-independent primitive, but prior stabilizer-subspace self-testing results were limited mainly to the five-qubit code. Extending these constructions to representative stabilizer codes would enable certification of encoded quantum information in a device-independent way.
method: The authors construct multipartite Bell inequalities adapted to stabilizer code structures and analyze their maximal quantum violations. They also introduce tilted sum-of-squares variants to impose algebraic constraints on logical-sector weights.
result: Maximal violations of the constructed Bell inequalities uniquely certify, up to local isometries, that the shared state lies within the logical subspace of the target code. The constructions cover the six-qubit code, the Steane code, and Shor's nine-qubit code, extending earlier five-qubit-code results.
conclusion: The work provides explicit examples of device-independent self-testing for representative stabilizer-code logical subspaces and suggests applications to verification and benchmarking of encoded quantum information.

title: The Three Kinds Of Three-qubit Entanglement
authors: Szilárd Szalay
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2242 (2026).

We construct an important missing piece in the entanglement theory of pure three-qubit states, which is a polynomial measure of W-entanglement. This works in parallel to the three-tangle, which is a polynomial measure of GHZ-entanglement, and to the bipartite concurrence, which is a polynomial measure of bipartite entanglement. We also show that these entanglement measures are ordered, the bipartite measure is larger than the W measure, which is larger than the GHZ measure. It is meaningful then to consider these three types of three-qubit entanglement, which are also ordered, bipartite is weaker than W, which is weaker than GHZ, in parallel to the order of the three kinds of equivalence classes of entangled three-qubit states.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a polynomial measure of W-entanglement for pure three-qubit states and establishes an ordering among bipartite, W, and GHZ entanglement measures.
motivation: Three-qubit entanglement theory lacked a polynomial measure for W-type entanglement analogous to the three-tangle for GHZ-type entanglement and concurrence for bipartite entanglement.
method: The author constructs a polynomial entanglement measure for W-class pure three-qubit states and compares it structurally and quantitatively with the three-tangle and bipartite concurrence.
result: The three measures are ordered: bipartite concurrence is larger than the W measure, which is larger than the GHZ measure, mirroring the ordering of the corresponding entanglement classes.
conclusion: This completes a missing piece in pure three-qubit entanglement theory and clarifies the hierarchy among bipartite, W, and GHZ entanglement.

title: Work Statistics Of Sudden Quantum Quenches: A Random Matrix Theory Perspective On Gaussianity And Its Deviations
authors: Miguel Tierz
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2241 (2026).

We show that, for sudden quenches, the work distribution reduces to the statistics of the traces of powers of Haar unitaries, which are random unitary matrices drawn uniformly from the unitary group. For translation-invariant quadratic fermionic chains with interactions extending to [MATH] neighbors and periodic boundary conditions, the Loschmidt amplitude admits a unitary matrix model / Toeplitz representation, which yields a work variable of the form [MATH] (and in models with pairing terms -superconducting pairing- additional [MATH] terms appear). By invoking multivariate central limit theorems for vectors of traces of unitaries, we obtain a Gaussian distribution for [MATH] with variance [MATH] and asymptotic independence across different powers. We also characterise the conditions under which non-Gaussian tails arise, for example from many interaction terms or their slow decay, as well as the appearance of Fisher-Hartwig singularities. We illustrate these mechanisms in the XY chain. Various numerical diagnostics support the analytical results.

.
tldr: The paper derives work statistics for sudden quantum quenches using random matrix theory, showing when the work distribution becomes Gaussian and characterizing non-Gaussian deviations.
motivation: Work statistics after sudden quenches are central to non-equilibrium quantum thermodynamics, but general analytical characterizations of their distribution are challenging. The paper aims to identify universal Gaussian behavior and mechanisms for deviations using random unitary matrix statistics.
method: For translation-invariant quadratic fermionic chains with finite-range interactions, the Loschmidt amplitude is mapped to a unitary matrix model/Toeplitz representation, reducing work variables to traces of powers of Haar unitaries. Multivariate central limit theorems then yield Gaussian work statistics and conditions for non-Gaussian tails.
result: The work distribution is shown to be Gaussian with variance determined by the random-matrix trace statistics, with asymptotic independence across powers, while non-Gaussian tails arise from many interaction terms, slow decay, or Fisher-Hartwig singularities. These mechanisms are illustrated in the XY chain and supported numerically.
conclusion: Random matrix theory provides a systematic framework for understanding Gaussianity and deviations in quench work statistics, linking quantum thermodynamic fluctuations to universal properties of Haar unitary traces.

title: Strict Hierarchy Between $n$-wise Measurement Simulability, Compatibility Structures, And Multi-copy Compatibility
authors: Lucas Tendick, Costantino Budroni, And Marco Túlio Quintino
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2231 (2026).

The incompatibility of quantum measurements, i.e. the fact that certain observable quantities cannot be measured jointly is widely regarded as a distinctive quantum feature with important implications for the foundations and the applications of quantum information theory. While the standard incompatibility of multiple measurements has been the focus of attention since the inception of quantum theory, its generalizations, such as measurement simulability, [MATH]-wise incompatibility, and mulit-copy incompatibility have only been proposed recently. Here, we point out that all these generalizations are differing notions of the question of how many measurements are genuinely contained in a measurement device. We then show, that all notions do differ not only in their operational meaning but also mathematically in the set of measurement assemblages they describe. We then fully resolve the relations between these different generalizations, by showing a strict hierarchy between these notions. Hence, we provide a general framework for generalized measurement incompatibility. Finally, we consider the implications our results have for recent works using these different notions.

.
tldr: The paper establishes a strict hierarchy among generalized notions of measurement incompatibility, including n-wise measurement simulability, compatibility structures, and multi-copy compatibility.
motivation: Generalized forms of measurement incompatibility have been introduced recently, but their operational meanings and mathematical relations were unclear, motivating a unified framework.
method: The authors compare the sets of measurement assemblages described by different generalized incompatibility notions and prove strict inclusions and separations among them.
result: They fully resolve the relations between these notions by showing a strict hierarchy, demonstrating that the generalizations differ both operationally and mathematically.
conclusion: The work provides a general framework for generalized measurement incompatibility and clarifies implications for prior and future applications of these concepts.

title: Fast Bosonic Control Via Multiphoton Qubit-Oscillator Interactions
authors: Noah Gorgichuk, Mohammad Ayyash, Matteo Mariantoni, And Sahel Ashhab
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2224 (2026).

We study the problem of [MATH]-fold rotationally symmetric bosonic state preparation, which is of great importance to bosonic quantum error correction, using a multiphoton interaction between an oscillator and an auxiliary qubit. We present an [MATH]-photon Law-Eberly ([MATH]LE) protocol that serves as an analytic baseline, alongside numerical optimal control calculations that further reduce state preparation time. We find that multiphoton control protocols substantially reduce preparation times for binomial, cat, and Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill codewords compared to schemes relying on standard linear interactions. Further, we achieve arbitrary control over the oscillator's Hilbert space by combining different multiphoton interaction orders. We also extend these control improvements to the preparation of rotationally symmetric multi-oscillator states. Lastly, numerical simulations using realistic planar superconducting circuit parameters validate the robustness of our scheme against qubit and oscillator decoherence. Our findings can significantly enhance the performance of bosonic codes on planar superconducting hardware, an important ingredient for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computers.

.
tldr: The paper presents multiphoton qubit-oscillator interaction protocols for fast preparation of rotationally symmetric bosonic code states, validated with realistic superconducting circuit parameters.
motivation: Bosonic quantum error correction requires fast and reliable preparation of nonclassical oscillator states, but standard linear qubit-oscillator interactions can be too slow for scalable fault-tolerant operation.
method: The authors introduce an N-photon Law-Eberly protocol as an analytic baseline and use numerical optimal control to further shorten state-preparation times, combining different multiphoton interaction orders and simulating decoherence with planar superconducting circuit parameters.
result: Multiphoton control substantially reduces preparation times for binomial, cat, and Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill codewords compared with linear-interaction schemes, enables arbitrary oscillator Hilbert-space control, and extends to multi-oscillator states while remaining robust against qubit and oscillator decoherence.
conclusion: Multiphoton qubit-oscillator interactions offer a promising route to faster bosonic code state preparation on superconducting hardware, supporting scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Asymptotically Good Bosonic Fock State Codes
authors: Dor Elimelech, Arda Aydin, And Alexander Barg
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2240 (2026).

We study the error-correction properties of multi-mode Fock-state codes under amplitude-damping (AD) noise, focusing on the asymptotic regime in which the total excitation of the code states grows without limit and the number of photon losses induced by the noise scales linearly with it. In this setting, existing code families, which correct only sublinearly many photon losses, do not protect against amplitude-damping (AD) noise with a constant loss parameter. As our main result, we address this gap by constructing asymptotically good Fock-state codes relying on random classical codes in the discrete simplex. Unlike many standard constructions of random quantum codes, our construction introduces randomness through the underlying classical indexing structure. Randomization also enables another desirable feature: bounded per-mode occupancy, which limits the number of photons in any individual mode and thereby increases the coherence lifetime of the code states. Finally, via a relation between Fock-state codes and permutation-invariant codes, our results also yield asymptotically good families of qudit permutation-invariant codes as well as codes in monolithic nuclear state spaces.

.
tldr: The paper constructs asymptotically good multi-mode bosonic Fock-state codes that correct a linear (constant-rate) number of photon losses under amplitude-damping noise, with bounded per-mode photon occupancy.
motivation: Existing Fock-state code families correct only a sublinear number of photon losses, so they fail to protect against amplitude damping with a constant loss parameter in the regime where the code's total excitation grows without limit.
method: The authors build code families by introducing randomness via random classical codes in the discrete simplex, which yields good error-correction properties while keeping per-mode occupancy bounded, and they exploit a relation between Fock-state codes and permutation-invariant codes.
result: The construction gives asymptotically good Fock-state codes for constant-rate amplitude damping, bounded per-mode photon number (improving coherence lifetime), and as a corollary asymptotically good qudit permutation-invariant codes and codes in monolithic nuclear state spaces.
conclusion: Randomization through the classical indexing structure closes the gap in bosonic Fock-state coding and provides a transferable route to good permutation-invariant codes relevant to bosonic and nuclear-spin quantum memories.

title: Approach To Optimal Quantum Transport Via States Over Time
authors: Matt Hoogsteder-Riera, John Calsamiglia, And Andreas Winter
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2236 (2026).

We approach the problem of constructing a quantum analogue of the immensely fruitful classical transport cost theory of Monge from a new angle. Going back to the original motivations, by which the transport is a bilinear function of a mass distribution (without loss of generality a probability density) and a transport plan (a stochastic kernel), we explore the quantum version where the mass distribution is generalised to a density matrix, and the transport plan to a completely positive and trace preserving map. These two data are naturally integrated into their Jordan product, which is called state over time (“stote''), and the transport cost is postulated to be a linear function of it. We explore the properties of this transport cost, as well as the optimal transport cost between two given states (simply the minimum cost over all suitable transport plans). After that, we analyse in considerable detail the case of unitary invariant cost, for which we can calculate many costs analytically. These findings suggest that our quantum transport cost is qualitatively different from Monge's classical transport.

.
tldr: The paper develops a quantum analogue of Monge's classical transport cost theory using density matrices, CPTP maps, and their Jordan product as a 'state over time'.
motivation: Classical optimal transport is powerful, but a quantum version remains subtle because mass distributions and transport plans must be replaced by states and quantum channels. The authors revisit Monge's original bilinear formulation to define a natural quantum transport cost.
method: They generalize mass distributions to density matrices and transport plans to completely positive trace-preserving maps, integrate them via the Jordan product into a state over time, and postulate the transport cost as a linear functional of this object. They then analyze properties and solve cases with unitary-invariant cost analytically.
result: The proposed transport cost is characterized, optimal transport between states is defined as a minimization over suitable CPTP maps, and many analytically tractable costs are obtained for unitary-invariant settings.
conclusion: The quantum transport cost exhibits qualitatively different behavior from classical Monge transport, suggesting a genuinely quantum optimal-transport framework with potential use in quantum information theory.

title: Composable Logical Gate Error In Approximate Quantum Error Correction: Reexamining Gate Implementations In Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill Codes
authors: Lukas Brenner, Beatriz Dias, And Robert Koenig
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2230 (2026).

Quantifying the accuracy of logical gates is paramount in approximate error correction, where perfect implementations are often unachievable with the available set of physical operations. To this end, we introduce a single scalar quantity we call the (composable) logical gate error. It captures both the deviation of the logical action from the desired target gate as well as leakage out of the code space. It is subadditive under successive application of gates, providing a simple means for analyzing circuits. We show how to bound the composable logical gate error in terms of matrix elements of physical unitaries between (approximate) logical computational basis states. In the continuous-variable context, this sidesteps the need for computing energy-bounded norms. As an example, we study the composable logical gate error for linear optics implementations of Paulis and Cliffords in approximate Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes. We find that the logical gate error for implementations of Paulis depends linearly on the squeezing parameter. This implies that their accuracy improves monotonically with the amount of squeezing. For some Cliffords, however, linear optics implementations which are exact for ideal GKP codes fail in the approximate case: they have a constant logical gate error even in the limit of infinite squeezing. This is consistent with previous results about the limitations of certain gate implementations for approximate GKP codes. It shows that findings applicable to ideal GKP codes do not always translate to the realm of physically realizable approximate GKP codes.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a composable logical gate error metric for approximate quantum error correction and applies it to linear-optics implementations of Paulis and Cliffords in approximate GKP codes.
motivation: Logical gate accuracy in approximate error correction is difficult to quantify because physical implementations are imperfect and leakage out of the code space must be accounted for.
method: The authors define a single scalar composable logical gate error that captures target-gate deviation and code-space leakage, prove subadditivity under gate composition, and bound it using matrix elements between approximate logical computational basis states.
result: For approximate GKP codes, Pauli gate errors scale linearly with the squeezing parameter and improve monotonically with squeezing, while some Clifford implementations that are exact for ideal GKP codes have constant error even at infinite squeezing.
conclusion: The composable logical gate error provides a practical circuit-analysis tool for approximate QEC, and results valid for ideal GKP codes do not always carry over to physically realizable approximate GKP codes.

title: Quantum Graph Theory By Example
authors: Gian Luca Spitzer And Ion Nechita
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2228 (2026).

Quantum graphs have been introduced by Duan, Severini, and Winter to describe the zero-error behaviour of quantum channels. Since then, quantum graph theory has become a field of study in its own right. A substantial source of difficulty in working with quantum graphs compared to classical graphs stems from the fact that they are no longer discrete objects. This makes it generally difficult to construct insightful, non-trivial examples. We present a collection of non-trivial quantum graphs that can be thought of in discrete terms, and that can be expressed in the diagrammatic formalism introduced by Musto, Reutter, and Verdon. The examples arise as the quantum graphs acted on by increasingly smaller classical matrix groups, and are parametrised by triples of matrices [MATH]. The parametrisation reveals a clean decomposition of quantum graph structure into classical and genuinely quantum components: [MATH] and [MATH] are described by a classical weighted graph called the strange graph, while [MATH] provides a purely quantum contribution with no classical analogue. Based on this model, we give exact formulas or establish bounds for quantum graph parameters, such as the number of connected components, the chromatic number, the independence number, and the clique number. Our results provide the first large, parametric families of quantum graphs for which standard graph parameters can be computed analytically.

.
tldr: The paper constructs parametric families of non-trivial quantum graphs arising from classical matrix group actions and analytically computes standard graph parameters for them.
motivation: Quantum graphs describe zero-error communication over quantum channels but are difficult to work with because they are non-discrete objects, making insightful examples scarce.
method: The authors parametrize quantum graphs by triples of matrices associated with increasingly smaller classical matrix groups and express them in the Musto-Reutter-Verdon diagrammatic formalism, separating classical and purely quantum structure.
result: They obtain exact formulas or bounds for connected components, chromatic number, independence number, and clique number, yielding the first large parametric families of quantum graphs with analytically computable standard parameters.
conclusion: The work provides a practical discrete-style toolkit for quantum graph theory and clarifies how classical and genuinely quantum graph structure can be decomposed.

title: A Quantum Optical Concept Of Attosecond Pulses: The Attoquants
authors: Varró Sándor And Gombkötő Ákos
abstract: High-harmonic generation (HHG) is conventionally understood to produce attosecond pulse trains only when the emitted harmonics are mutually phase-locked, in accordance with the classical theory of mode-locking. In a quantum optical framework, pulse synthesis would also require a regular phase relation between the components, when the harmonic field is in a separable multimode quantum state. This requirement, however, can be circumvented for harmonic combs exhibiting intermodal entanglement. We introduce a novel family of multimode quantum states, termed attoquants: states associated with highly structured pulse trains that are inherently insensitive to relative phases. As a concrete example, we analyse the coherent permanent state, constructed as a completely symmetric superposition of products of coherent states over all permutations of a fixed parameter set. It is shown analytically that its electric-field mean value is a locked Fourier superposition of the driving-field harmonics, yielding an attosecond pulse train without requiring regular phase relations between the high-harmonic components. We further calculate the photon statistics, the Wigner function, and the logarithmic negativity of these states, in order to show their genuinely nonclassical character, and the degree of entanglement. Finally, we offer a phenomenological interpretation for the generation of such entangled states during HHG, as a consequence of multi-atom effects. Since the coherence volume of the driving field greatly exceeds that of its harmonics, a collectively-driven cluster of atoms can radiate the harmonics as spatially separated, but classically indistinguishable sources. This can generate the permutation-symmetric entanglement structure of an attoquant.
tldr: The paper introduces 'attoquants', multimode entangled quantum states that enable phase-insensitive attosecond pulse trains from high-harmonic generation.
motivation: Conventional high-harmonic generation is thought to produce attosecond pulse trains only when harmonics are phase-locked, but intermodal entanglement may circumvent this requirement in a quantum optical framework.
method: The authors define a coherent permanent state as a permutation-symmetric superposition of multimode coherent states and analytically compute its electric-field mean value, photon statistics, Wigner function, and logarithmic negativity.
result: The coherent permanent state yields a locked Fourier superposition and an attosecond pulse train without requiring regular phase relations between harmonics, while exhibiting genuinely nonclassical character and intermodal entanglement.
conclusion: Intermodal entanglement can replace phase locking in attosecond pulse synthesis, and attoquants provide a novel family of multimode quantum states with potential relevance to entanglement theory and quantum optics.

title: Quantum Walks On Arbitrary Spatial Networks With Rydberg Atoms
authors: Gabriel Almeida, Raul Santos, Lara Janiurek, And Yasser Omar
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2235 (2026).

Rydberg atoms provide a highly promising platform for quantum computation, leveraging their strong tunable interactions to encode and manipulate information in the electronic states of individual atoms. Key advantages of Rydberg atoms include scalability, reconfigurable connectivity, and native multi-qubit gates, making them particularly well-suited for addressing complex network problems. These problems can often be framed as graph-based tasks, which can be efficiently addressed using quantum walks. In this work, we propose a general implementation of staggered quantum walks with Rydberg atoms, with a particular focus on spatial networks. We also present an efficient algorithm for constructing the tessellations required for the staggered quantum walk. Finally, we demonstrate that our proposal achieves performance consistent with a quadratic speedup in spatial search algorithms.

.
tldr: The paper proposes a Rydberg-atom implementation of staggered quantum walks on arbitrary spatial networks, including an efficient tessellation-construction algorithm and evidence of quadratic speedup for spatial search.
motivation: Rydberg atoms offer scalable, reconfigurable connectivity and strong tunable interactions, making them attractive for graph-based quantum information tasks such as quantum walks and spatial search.
method: The authors design a general scheme for staggered quantum walks using Rydberg-atom arrays and provide an efficient algorithm to construct the required tessellations for arbitrary spatial networks.
result: They demonstrate that the proposal achieves performance consistent with a quadratic speedup in spatial search algorithms on the target networks.
conclusion: The work shows that Rydberg-atom platforms can implement network-based quantum walks and may enable practical quantum-enhanced graph search, though it remains an implementation proposal rather than an experimental demonstration.

title: Rare Event Simulation Of Quantum Error-Correcting Circuits
authors: Carolyn Mayer, Anand Ganti, Uzoma Onunkwo, Tzvetan Metodi, Benjamin Anker, And Jacek Skryzalin
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2237 (2026).

We describe a practical approach for accessing the logical failure rates of quantum error-correcting (QEC) circuits under low physical (component) failure rate regimes. Standard Monte Carlo is often the de facto approach for studying the failure rates of quantum circuits. However, in the study of fault-tolerant error-correcting circuits, the ability to extend this approach to low physical failure rates is limited. In particular, the use of Monte Carlo to access circuits that are relatively large or have high correcting power becomes more difficult as we lower the input failure rates of the individual components (gates) in the circuit. For these reasons, many simulations studying the circuit model go no lower than end-to-end logical failure rates in the [MATH] regime. In this report, we outline an approach that borrows from earlier work by Bravyi and Vargo [6] to the more complex circuit noise model. Earlier works studied both the capacity and phenomenological noise models [6,3,5], but the work is insufficient for generating similar simulations in the circuit-noise model. To the best of our knowledge, our team is the first to develop a full prescription of the rare event simulation by splitting technique for the circuit-based noise model. We have also generated promising results that are confirmed by standard Monte Carlo simulation under an accessible regime. This work shows that we can access noise in the circuit-model prescription of quantum error-correcting code to failure rates below [MATH] regime.

.
tldr: The paper develops a rare-event simulation method for estimating logical failure rates of quantum error-correcting circuits under circuit-level noise at low physical failure rates.
motivation: Standard Monte Carlo simulation becomes impractical for accessing low logical failure rates in large or high-correcting-power fault-tolerant QEC circuits, limiting studies of circuit-level noise to relatively high end-to-end failure rates.
method: The authors adapt the Bravyi-Vargo rare-event simulation by splitting technique from simpler noise models to the circuit-based noise model and validate the approach against standard Monte Carlo in an accessible regime.
result: They provide, to their knowledge, the first full prescription of rare-event simulation by splitting for the circuit-based noise model and show that it can access logical failure rates below regimes reachable by standard Monte Carlo.
conclusion: Rare-event simulation enables practical estimation of logical failure rates for QEC circuits at low physical error rates, extending fault-tolerance studies beyond standard Monte Carlo limitations.

title: Scalable Long-distance Quantum Fan-out Gates With Reduced Resource Overhead
authors: Wen-Qiang Liu And Hai-Rui Wei
abstract: Scalable long-distance quantum gates are essential for distributed quantum computation and scalable quantum networks. We propose an efficient scheme for implementing an -qubit fan-out gate (also known as a controlled-NOT- -NOT gate) across spatially separated parties. Our protocol requires only a pre-shared -qubit Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger state, local controlled-NOT (CNOT) gates, and feed-forward operations, thereby reducing both the CNOT and Hadamard gate counts by when compared with the standard decomposition-based approach. We further develop two optical architectures to implement the heralded and post-selected -photon fan-out gates, respectively. These schemes require fewer single photons resources and achieve higher success probabilities than their decomposition-based counterparts, representing significant improvements. The results indicate that our approach is experimentally feasible and pave the way toward practical long-distance quantum computation.
tldr: The paper proposes a resource-efficient scheme for implementing long-distance multi-qubit fan-out gates across spatially separated parties using pre-shared GHZ states and local operations.
motivation: Scalable long-distance quantum gates are needed for distributed quantum computation and quantum networks, but standard decomposition-based implementations require many CNOT and Hadamard gates and large photonic resource overhead.
method: The protocol uses a pre-shared n-qubit GHZ state, local CNOT gates, and feed-forward operations to realize an n-qubit fan-out gate, and develops heralded and post-selected optical architectures for n-photon fan-out gates.
result: The scheme reduces CNOT and Hadamard gate counts significantly compared with standard decompositions and achieves fewer single-photon resource requirements and higher success probabilities in the optical implementations.
conclusion: The approach provides an experimentally feasible route toward practical long-distance quantum computation and scalable quantum network primitives, though it remains a protocol-level proposal without experimental demonstration.

title: Leggett–Garg Inequality Violation In Muon G–2 Experiments
authors: Morgan Cassidy And Kun Cheng Brian Batell
abstract: We present the first study of Leggett–Garg inequality (LGI) violation in polarized muon spin precession. We formulate a procedure to reconstruct temporal correlators of the longitudinal muon polarization from measured time-dependent muon decay spectra and apply it to publicly available Fermilab Muon data corresponding to approximately billion muon decays. Using a simplified model of the detector acceptance and efficiency, the LGI is found to be violated with a single-bin significance of , while combining neighboring bins further increases the significance. While our analysis is limited by systematic uncertainties associated with the detector modeling, a dedicated experimental analysis could reduce these uncertainties toward the statistical level, , potentially enabling one of the most precise measurements of temporal quantum correlations.
tldr: The paper presents the first study of Leggett-Garg inequality violation in polarized muon spin precession using publicly available Fermilab Muon g-2 data.
motivation: Leggett-Garg inequalities test temporal quantum correlations and macrorealism, providing a time-domain analogue of Bell inequality tests in a high-statistics muon system.
method: The authors reconstruct temporal correlators of longitudinal muon polarization from measured time-dependent muon decay spectra and apply the procedure to approximately billions of muon decays using a simplified detector acceptance and efficiency model.
result: The Leggett-Garg inequality is found to be violated with a single-bin significance, and combining neighboring bins further increases the significance, though detector-model systematics currently limit the analysis.
conclusion: A dedicated experimental analysis could reduce systematic uncertainties toward the statistical level, potentially enabling one of the most precise measurements of temporal quantum correlations.

title: Universal Dilation Of Linear Itô SDEs: Quantum Trajectories And Lindblad Simulation Of Second Moments
authors: Hsuan-Cheng Wu And Xiantao Li
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2223 (2026).

We present a universal framework for simulating [MATH]-dimensional linear Itô stochastic differential equations (SDEs) on quantum computers with additive or multiplicative noises. Building on a unitary dilation technique, we establish a rigorous mapping from the general linear SDEs [MATH] to stochastic Schrödinger equations (SSE) on a dilated Hilbert space. Crucially, this embedding is pathwise exact in that the classical solution is recovered as a projection of the dilated quantum state for each fixed noise realization. We demonstrate that the resulting SSEs are naturally implementable on digital quantum processors, where the stochastic Wiener increments are encoded directly by preparing the ancillary qubits. Exploiting this physical mapping, we develop two algorithmic strategies: (1) a trajectory-based approach that uses sequential weak measurements to realize efficient stochastic integrators, including a second-order scheme, and (2) an ensemble-based approach that maps moment evolution to a deterministic Lindblad quantum master equation, enabling simulation without Monte Carlo sampling. We provide error bounds based on a stochastic light-cone analysis and validate the framework with numerical experiments.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a unitary-dilation framework for simulating linear Itô SDEs on quantum computers via stochastic Schrödinger equations and Lindblad master equations for second moments.
motivation: Efficient simulation of classical stochastic differential equations and their moment evolution is challenging, and quantum processors may offer new algorithmic routes via open-quantum-system embeddings.
method: Linear Itô SDEs are mapped pathwise exactly to stochastic Schrödinger equations on a dilated Hilbert space, with Wiener increments encoded in ancilla qubits; the authors develop trajectory-based weak-measurement integrators and an ensemble-based Lindblad simulation of second moments.
result: The mapping is exact for each noise realization, the resulting algorithms are implementable on digital quantum processors, and error bounds are derived via stochastic light-cone analysis with numerical validation.
conclusion: This provides a rigorous quantum-simulation framework for linear SDEs and deterministic Lindblad evolution of moments, avoiding Monte Carlo sampling in the ensemble approach.

title: Performance Of The Spin Qubit Shuttling Architecture For A Surface Code Implementation
authors: Berat Yenilen, Arnau Sala, Hendrik Bluhm, Markus Müller, And Manuel Rispler
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2219 (2026).

Qubit shuttling promises to advance some quantum computing platforms to the qubit register sizes needed for effective quantum error correction (QEC), but also introduces additional errors whose impact must be evaluated. The established method to investigate the performance of QEC codes in a realistic scenario is to employ a standard noise model known as circuit-level noise, where all quantum operations are modeled as noisy. In the present work, we take this noise model and single out the effect of shuttling errors by introducing them as an additional so-called error location. This hardware abstraction is motivated by the SpinBus architecture and allows a systematic numerical investigation to map out the resulting two-dimensional parameter space. To this end, we take the Surface code and perform large scale simulations, most notably extracting the threshold across said two-dimensional parameter space. We study two scenarios for shuttling errors, depolarization on the one hand and dephasing on the other hand. For a purely dephasing shuttling error, we find a threshold of several percent, provided that all other operations have a high fidelity. The qubit overhead needed to reach a logical error rate of [MATH] (known as the "teraquop" regime [23] increases only moderately for shuttling error rates up to about 1 % per shuttling operation. The error rates at which practically useful, i.e. well below threshold error correction is predicted to be possible are comfortably higher than what is expected to be achievable for spin qubits. Our results thus show that it is reasonable to expect shuttling operations to fall below threshold already at surprisingly large error rates. With realistic efforts in the near term, this offers positive prospects for spin qubit based quantum processors as a viable avenue for scalable fault-tolerant error-corrected quantum computing.

.
tldr: Large-scale circuit-level simulations of the surface code under spin-qubit shuttling noise show that thresholds of several percent are attainable, making shuttling-based spin-qubit architectures viable for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
motivation: Qubit shuttling can scale spin-qubit registers to the sizes required for effective quantum error correction, but it introduces additional error mechanisms whose impact on code performance has not been systematically quantified.
method: The authors extend the standard circuit-level noise model by adding shuttling as an extra error location motivated by the SpinBus architecture, then perform large-scale surface-code simulations over a two-dimensional parameter space for both depolarizing and dephasing shuttling errors, extracting thresholds and logical-error-rate overheads.
result: For purely dephasing shuttling errors the threshold reaches several percent when other operations are high-fidelity, and the qubit overhead needed to reach the teraquop regime grows only moderately for shuttling error rates up to about 1% per operation.
conclusion: Practically useful error correction appears achievable at shuttling error rates comfortably above what spin-qubit hardware is expected to deliver, supporting shuttling-based spin-qubit processors as a promising route to scalable fault tolerance.

title: Unitary Causal Decompositions: A Characterisation Via Lattice Theory
authors: Tein van der Lugt And Robin Lorenz
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2218 (2026).

If a unitary transformation has a circuit representation with no directed path from input [MATH] to output [MATH], then [MATH] does not influence [MATH] through the overall unitary. Conversely, if a unitary satisfies a number of no-influence conditions, it is natural to wonder whether a circuit decomposition exists in which all of them are represented by absences of paths. Such decompositions are known as causal decompositions; determining their existence in general is a central open problem in the study of causal structure in quantum theory. We present progress towards a general solution by considering the special case of unitary causal decompositions, i.e. decompositions in terms of unitary circuits in the traditional quantum circuit formalism that do not require the generalisation to 'extended' or 'routed' quantum circuits prompted by earlier research on this topic. We identify a combinatorial condition that characterises precisely those sets of no-influence constraints [MATH] for which any unitary transformation satisfying [MATH] admits a unitary causal decomposition representing the constraints. Our approach is systematic, grounded in lattice theory and finite-dimensional operator algebra, and offers hope for extensions to more general (e.g. routed unitary) causal decompositions in the future.

.
tldr: The paper characterizes when sets of no-influence constraints on a unitary transformation admit a unitary causal decomposition, using lattice theory and finite-dimensional operator algebra.
motivation: Causal decompositions formalize the correspondence between absent influence relations and absent paths in a quantum circuit, and determining their existence is a central open problem in quantum causal structure.
method: The authors restrict to unitary causal decompositions in the standard quantum circuit formalism and identify a combinatorial condition via lattice-theoretic and operator-algebraic methods.
result: They obtain a precise combinatorial characterization of exactly those no-influence constraint sets for which every unitary satisfying the constraints has a unitary causal decomposition representing them.
conclusion: This provides systematic progress on causal decompositions and suggests a route toward more general routed or extended unitary causal decompositions.

title: Compound Beams For Direct Experimental Comparison Of Quantum Operations
authors: Kishore Thapliyal, Jan Peřina Jr, Pavel Pavlíček And Antonín Černoch
abstract: Compound beams composed of simple experimental blocks (detected in simultaneous detection windows) that form specific quantum-correlated structures are suggested for simulating the properties of different quantum operations used for creating highly nonclassical and entangled multi-mode states needed in quantum communication, metrology, and information protocols. Qualitative and quantitative comparison of multi-photon addition (PA) and subtraction in compound multi-mode thermal as well as sub-Poissonian beams and multi-mode twin beams with their intensities extending over two orders in magnitude is provided. Adding and subtracting up to twenty photocounts, optimal conditions for the generation of experimental nonclassical states are identified. In general, PA is identified as advantageous over photon subtraction (PS) for the multi-mode thermal and sub-Poissonian beams: It induces (enhances) the nonclassicality in the former (latter) state. Contrary to this, PS outperforms PA in the multi-mode twin beams. Moreover, exploiting temporal photon-pair correlations in compound twin beams when post-selecting, nearly ideal experimental photon(s) addition is demonstrated. The results apply for the beams with mean photon number per mode much less than one.
tldr: The paper experimentally compares multi-photon addition and subtraction in compound multi-mode beams, identifying conditions where each operation best generates nonclassical states.
motivation: Nonclassical and entangled multi-mode states are needed for quantum communication, metrology, and information protocols, motivating a direct comparison of state-generation operations.
method: Using compound beams detected in simultaneous windows, the authors compare multi-photon addition and subtraction up to twenty photocounts in multi-mode thermal, sub-Poissonian, and twin beams.
result: Photon addition is advantageous for thermal and sub-Poissonian beams, while photon subtraction outperforms it for twin beams; temporal photon-pair correlations enable nearly ideal post-selected photon addition.
conclusion: The work provides experimental guidance for choosing photon addition versus subtraction when engineering nonclassical multi-mode states at low mean photon number per mode.

title: Variational Perturbation Theory In Open Quantum Systems For Efficient Steady State Computation
authors: André Melo, Gaspard Beugnot, And Fabrizio Minganti
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2246 (2026).

Determining the steady state of an open quantum system is crucial for characterizing quantum devices and studying various physical phenomena. Often, computing a single steady state is insufficient, and it is necessary to explore its dependence on multiple external parameters. In such cases, calculating the steady state independently for each combination of parameters quickly becomes intractable. Perturbation theory (PT) can mitigate this challenge by expanding steady states around reference parameters, minimizing redundant computations across neighboring parameter values. However, PT has two significant limitations: it relies on the pseudo-inverse – a numerically costly operation – and has a limited radius of convergence. In this work, we remove both of these roadblocks. First, we introduce a variational perturbation theory (VPT) and its multipoint generalization that significantly extends the radius of convergence even in the presence of non-analytic effects such as dissipative phase transitions. Then, we develop two numerical strategies that eliminate the need to compute pseudo-inverses. The first relies on a single LU decomposition to efficiently construct the steady state within the convergence region, while the second reformulates VPT as a Krylov space recycling problem and uses preconditioned iterative methods. We benchmark these approaches across various models, demonstrating their broad applicability and significant improvements over standard PT.

.
tldr: The paper introduces variational perturbation theory and numerical strategies to compute steady states of open quantum systems efficiently across parameter regimes.
motivation: Computing steady states independently for many parameter combinations is expensive, and standard perturbation theory is limited by costly pseudo-inverses and a small convergence radius.
method: The authors develop variational perturbation theory, including a multipoint generalization, and two pseudo-inverse-free numerical approaches based on LU decomposition and Krylov space recycling with preconditioned iterative methods.
result: Benchmarks show that the methods extend the convergence radius, handle non-analytic effects such as dissipative phase transitions, and significantly outperform standard perturbation theory.
conclusion: The approach provides a practical computational tool for exploring parameter-dependent steady states of open quantum systems, with broad applicability to quantum device characterization.

title: Chaotic Scattering In Ultracold Atom-ion Collisions
authors: Meirav Pinkas, Jonathan Wengrowicz, Nitzan Akerman And Roee Ozeri
abstract: We report on signatures of classical chaos in ultracold collisions between a trapped ion and a free atom. Using numerical simulations, we show that the scattering dynamics can be highly sensitive to initial conditions for various mass ratios and trapping frequencies, indicating the onset of chaos. We quantify this chaotic dynamics by calculating its fractal dimension. We show that for a trapped Sr ion and a free Rb atom chaotic dynamic appears under experimentally relevant conditions, and find its characteristic energy scale. The observation of classical chaos in atom-trapped-ion collisions suggests that signatures of quantum chaos might appear, for example, through a Wigner–Dyson distribution of collisional resonances.
tldr: Numerical simulations reveal signatures of classical chaos in ultracold collisions between a trapped ion and a free atom, with possible implications for quantum chaos in atom-ion hybrid systems.
motivation: The authors aim to characterize the scattering dynamics of trapped-ion/free-atom collisions, which are relevant to hybrid atom-ion platforms, and to identify whether chaotic behavior emerges under experimentally realistic conditions.
method: They perform numerical simulations of ultracold collisions across various mass ratios and trapping frequencies, quantify sensitivity to initial conditions, and compute the fractal dimension of the scattering dynamics.
result: For a trapped Sr ion colliding with a free Rb atom, chaotic dynamics appears under experimentally relevant conditions, and the authors identify a characteristic energy scale; they further suggest that quantum chaos may manifest as a Wigner-Dyson distribution of collisional resonances.
conclusion: Classical chaos in atom-ion collisions may provide a route to observing quantum chaos signatures, which is relevant for understanding and controlling hybrid trapped-ion/neutral-atom systems.

title: Multi-echo Evaluation Of Non-invertible Errors In Target Quantum Computations
authors: Ivan Henao And Raam Uzdin Jader P Santos
abstract: This work introduces a method for quantifying errors in quantum computations using multiple echoes of a target circuit. Our approach addresses a gap in the range of available benchmarking methods: unlike existing approaches that evaluate the average performance of a device, circuit, or gate, our method estimates the error in a target computation using the same initial state and circuit as the computation itself. It therefore captures how noise manifests in the specific computation of interest. We present two variants of the approach. The first estimates incoherent errors through purity loss, while the second estimates the echo infidelity, which captures both incoherent errors and non-invertible coherent errors, such as crosstalk. The purity-loss method applies to low-error circuits, or layers of gates, regardless of system size. The echo-infidelity method applies to circuits of arbitrary size and remains effective even at high error rates. Because our approach does not rely on an explicit noise model, it can complement methods that provide more detailed error information by testing the validity of the sparsity assumptions underlying those models. Finally, we discuss platforms on which our method can be implemented immediately.
tldr: The paper introduces a multi-echo benchmarking method to estimate errors in a specific target quantum computation, separating incoherent purity loss from non-invertible coherent errors such as crosstalk.
motivation: Existing benchmarking methods typically measure average device, gate, or circuit performance rather than the error affecting the particular target computation, so they may miss computation-specific noise effects.
method: The approach uses multiple echoes of the target circuit. One variant estimates incoherent errors via purity loss, while another estimates echo infidelity to capture both incoherent and non-invertible coherent errors without relying on an explicit noise model.
result: The purity-loss method works for low-error circuits or gate layers regardless of system size, while the echo-infidelity method applies to arbitrary-size circuits and remains effective at high error rates; the approach can also test sparsity assumptions in noise models.
conclusion: The method provides a complementary, model-free tool for characterizing errors in specific quantum computations and is implementable on existing platforms, though its focus is benchmarking rather than core quantum information theory.

title: Universality Classes, Thermodynamics Of Group Entropies, And Black Holes
authors: Petr Jizba And Piergiulio Tempesta Henrik Jeldtoft Jensen
abstract: Conventional Boltzmann–Gibbs statistical mechanics successfully describes systems with weak to moderate correlations, in which the number of accessible configurations grows exponentially with the number of degrees of freedom . However, this framework breaks down for systems for which the effectively occupied configuration space exhibits non-exponential growth. While numerous generalized entropies have been proposed to address this limitation, a coherent link to classical thermodynamic laws has remained elusive. Here, we propose group entropies as a unifying framework, defining universality classes of entropies through the asymptotic scaling of , each yielding an extensive entropy. We show that this approach provides the basis for a consistent thermodynamic formulation beyond the Boltzmann–Gibbs paradigm. In particular, by expressing these entropies in terms of thermodynamic state variables, we demonstrate their consistency with classical thermodynamics, in close analogy to the emergence of the Clausius entropy from the Boltzmann–Gibbs formalism. Focusing on the zeroth thermodynamic law, we identify the empirical temperature and, by using Carathéodory’s formulation of the second law, we derive the associated absolute temperature. As an application, we analyse black-hole thermodynamics using the extensive group entropy class corresponding to stretched-exponential behaviour of and derive a negative heat capacity, known to be a hallmark property of black holes. This result holds for the stretched-exponential entropies associated with both the Bekenstein–Hawking and Barrow entropy scalings.
tldr: The paper proposes group entropies as a unifying framework for generalized statistical mechanics and derives a consistent thermodynamic formulation, applying it to black-hole thermodynamics.
motivation: Boltzmann-Gibbs statistical mechanics fails for systems with non-exponential configuration-space growth, and generalized entropies have lacked a coherent link to classical thermodynamic laws.
method: The authors define universality classes of entropies via asymptotic scaling of the group-entropy function, express them in thermodynamic state variables, and use Carathéodory's formulation of the second law to derive absolute temperature.
result: The group-entropy framework yields extensive entropies consistent with classical thermodynamics, and for stretched-exponential entropy classes it reproduces black-hole negative heat capacity for both Bekenstein-Hawking and Barrow scalings.
conclusion: Group entropies provide a systematic thermodynamic foundation beyond Boltzmann-Gibbs, with black-hole thermodynamics as a concrete application, though the work is classical/generalized rather than quantum-information focused.

title: Failure Of The Mean-field Hartree Approximation For A Bosonic Many-body System With non-Hermitian Hamiltonian
authors: Matias Ginzburg, Simone Rademacher, And Giacomo de Palma
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2244 (2026).

Mean-field Hartree theory is a central tool for reducing many-body dynamics to an effective one-particle evolution. This approximation has been employed when the Hamiltonian governing the many-body dynamics is not Hermitian. Indeed, non-Hermitian Hamiltonians model particle gain/loss or the evolution of open quantum systems between consecutive quantum jumps. Furthermore, the validity of the Hartree approximation for generic non-Hermitian Hamiltonians lies at the basis of a quantum algorithm for nonlinear differential equations. In this work, we show that this approximation can fail. First, we consider the most general bosonic mean-field Hamiltonian with two-body interactions and we prove that, for non-Hermitian Hamiltonian, the Hartree equation does not capture the correct second time derivative of the one-particle marginal state at [MATH] in the thermodynamic limit. Then, we analytically solve a model of [MATH] bosonic qubits with a purely anti-Hermitian Hamiltonian, compute the limit for [MATH] of the one-particle marginal state and show that it does not agree with the solution of the non-Hermitian Hartree equation. We further show that there exists an initial condition such that the exact one-particle marginal state undergoes a finite-time transition to a mixed state, a phenomenon that is completely absent in the case of Hermitian Hamiltonians. Finally, we simulate a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian with real spectrum and show that, also in this case, there are initial conditions for which the Hartree equation does not reproduce the correct one-particle marginal state in the limit [MATH]. Our findings challenge the validity of the mean-field Hartree approximation for non-Hermitian Hamiltonians, and call for additional conditions for the validity of the mean-field regime to model the dynamics of particle gain and loss and the open-system dynamics in bosonic many-body systems.

.
tldr: The paper shows that the mean-field Hartree approximation can fail for bosonic many-body systems governed by non-Hermitian Hamiltonians.
motivation: Non-Hermitian Hamiltonians describe particle gain/loss and open-system dynamics between quantum jumps, and the Hartree approximation is used in this context and in a quantum algorithm for nonlinear differential equations, so its validity needs scrutiny.
method: The authors analyze the most general bosonic mean-field Hamiltonian with two-body interactions, compare the exact second time derivative of the one-particle marginal state with the Hartree prediction, solve an anti-Hermitian bosonic-qubit model analytically, and simulate a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian with real spectrum.
result: They find that the non-Hermitian Hartree equation does not capture the correct short-time dynamics, the exact thermodynamic-limit one-particle marginal can disagree with the Hartree solution, and some initial conditions lead to a finite-time transition to a mixed state absent in Hermitian cases.
conclusion: The findings challenge the validity of the mean-field Hartree approximation for non-Hermitian bosonic systems and call for additional conditions when modeling gain/loss or open-system dynamics in the mean-field regime.

title: Enhanced Measurements On Quantum Computers Via The Simultaneous Probing Of Non-commuting Pauli Operators
authors: Rick P. A. Simon, Zheng Shi, Charlie Nation, Andrew Jena, And Luca Dellantonio
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2229 (2026).

Measuring the state of quantum computers is a highly non-trivial task, with implications for virtually all quantum algorithms. A promising avenue is multi-copy schemes, where identical copies of a quantum state are measured jointly so that all Pauli operators within the considered observable can be simultaneously assessed. Here, we present a first implementation of such a two-copy scheme in a measurement protocol. Based on Bayesian statistics, it accurately estimates not only the average of the desired observable but also the error en route. This enables an adaptive shot-allocation algorithm that preferentially samples the most uncertain Pauli terms. In regimes with many non-commuting Pauli operators, this “double'' scheme can outperform the state-of-the-art measurement protocol in minimizing total shots for a given precision. We also numerically confirm the finding in previous theoretical works that the two-copy scheme incurs an overhead due to the square-root relationship between the variance of measured quantities and the number of measurement shots.

.
tldr: The paper implements a two-copy Bayesian measurement protocol for simultaneously estimating non-commuting Pauli observables on quantum computers, with adaptive shot allocation.
motivation: Efficient measurement of observables is critical for quantum algorithms, and multi-copy schemes can jointly estimate non-commuting Pauli terms that cannot be measured simultaneously in standard single-copy sampling.
method: The authors present a first implementation of a two-copy measurement scheme based on Bayesian statistics, estimating both the observable average and the associated error, and use this to adaptively allocate shots to the most uncertain Pauli terms.
result: In regimes with many non-commuting Pauli operators, the two-copy scheme can outperform the state-of-the-art measurement protocol in minimizing total shots for a given precision, though it incurs a square-root variance overhead as predicted theoretically.
conclusion: The work demonstrates practical potential for enhanced observable estimation on quantum computers, but it is a specialized measurement/estimation protocol rather than a core contribution to the researcher's primary quantum information interests.

title: Symmetry Defects And Gauging For Quantum States With Matrix Product Unitary Symmetries
authors: Adrián Franco-Rubio, Arkadiusz Bochniak, And J. Ignacio Cirac
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2243 (2026).

In this work, we examine the consequences of the existence of a finite group of matrix product unitary (MPU) symmetries for matrix product states (MPS). We generalize the well-understood picture of onsite unitary symmetries, which give rise to virtual symmetry defects given by insertions of operators in the bonds of the MPS. In the MPU case, we can define analogous defect tensors, this time sitting on lattice sites, that can be created, moved, and fused by local unitary operators. We leverage this formalism to study the gauging of MPU symmetries. We introduce a condition, block independence, under which we can gauge the symmetries by promoting the symmetry defects to gauge degrees of freedom, yielding an MPS of the same bond dimension that supports a local version of the symmetry given by commuting gauge constraints. Whenever block independence does not hold (which happens, in particular, whenever the symmetry representation is anomalous), a modification of our method which we call state-level gauging still gives rise to a locally symmetric MPS by promotion of the symmetry defects, at the expense of producing gauge constraints that do not commute on different sites.

.
tldr: The paper develops a tensor-network formalism for symmetry defects and gauging of matrix product unitary symmetries in matrix product states.
motivation: It aims to generalize the well-understood picture of onsite unitary symmetries and virtual defects to the more general case of finite-group matrix product unitary symmetries acting on MPS.
method: The authors define defect tensors on lattice sites that can be created, moved, and fused by local unitaries, and introduce a block-independence condition for gauging by promoting defects to gauge degrees of freedom; a state-level gauging procedure handles anomalous or non-block-independent cases.
result: Under block independence, gauging produces an MPS of the same bond dimension with local commuting gauge constraints; otherwise state-level gauging yields a locally symmetric MPS but with gauge constraints that do not commute across sites.
conclusion: The work extends symmetry-defect and gauging techniques from onsite symmetries to MPU symmetries, providing a systematic MPS framework including anomalous cases.

title: Interactive Proofs For Verifying (quantum) Learning And Testing
authors: Matthias C. Caro, Jens Eisert, Marcel Hinsche, Marios Ioannou, Alexander Nietner, And Ryan Sweke
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2239 (2026).

We consider the problem of testing and learning from data in the presence of resource constraints, such as limited memory or weak data access, which place limitations on the efficiency and feasibility of testing or learning. In particular, we ask the following question: Could a resource-constrained learner/tester use interaction with a resource-unconstrained but untrusted party to solve a learning or testing problem more efficiently than they could without such an interaction? In this work, we answer this question both abstractly and for concrete problems, in two complementary ways: For a wide variety of scenarios, we prove that a resource-constrained learner cannot gain any advantage through classical interaction with an untrusted prover. As a special case, we show that for the vast majority of testing and learning problems in which quantum memory is a meaningful resource, a memory-constrained quantum algorithm cannot overcome its limitations via classical communication with a memory-unconstrained quantum prover. In contrast, when quantum communication is allowed, we construct a variety of interactive proof protocols, for specific learning and testing problems, which allow memory-constrained quantum verifiers to gain significant advantages through delegation to untrusted provers. These results highlight both the limitations and potential of delegating learning and testing problems to resource-rich but untrusted third parties.

.
tldr: The paper studies whether memory- or access-constrained quantum learners and testers can benefit from interacting with an untrusted but resource-unconstrained prover, showing classical interaction gives no advantage while quantum communication enables delegation protocols.
motivation: Resource constraints such as limited quantum memory or weak data access can make learning and testing inefficient, raising the question of whether an untrusted third party can help without compromising correctness.
method: The authors prove general no-advantage results for classical interaction with an untrusted prover and construct interactive proof protocols that exploit quantum communication for specific learning and testing tasks.
result: Classical interaction cannot overcome memory constraints for a broad class of learning and testing problems, whereas quantum communication allows memory-constrained verifiers to gain significant advantages via delegation.
conclusion: The work delineates the limitations and potential of delegating learning and testing to resource-rich untrusted parties, highlighting quantum communication as a key resource.

title: Quantum Algorithms For General Nonlinear Dynamics Based On The Carleman Embedding
authors: David Jennings, Kamil Korzekwa, Matteo Lostaglio, Andrew T Sornborger, Yigit Subasi, And Guoming Wang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2233 (2026).

Important nonlinear dynamics, such as those found in plasma and fluid systems, are typically hard to simulate on classical computers. Thus, if fault-tolerant quantum computers could efficiently solve such nonlinear problems, it would be a transformative change for many industries. In a recent breakthrough [Liu et al., PNAS 2021], the first efficient quantum algorithm for solving nonlinear differential equations was constructed, based on a single condition [MATH], where [MATH] characterizes the ratio of nonlinearity to dissipation. This result, however, is limited to the class of purely dissipative systems with negative log-norm, which excludes application to many important problems. In this work, we correct technical issues with this and other prior analysis, and substantially extend the scope of nonlinear dynamical systems that can be efficiently simulated on a quantum computer in a number of ways. Firstly, we extend the existing results from purely dissipative systems to a much broader class of stable systems, and show that every quadratic Lyapunov function for the linearized system corresponds to an independent [MATH]-number criterion for the convergence of the Carleman scheme. Secondly, we extend our stable system results to physically relevant settings where conserved polynomial quantities exist. Finally, we provide extensive results for the class of non-resonant systems. With this, we are able to show that efficient quantum algorithms exist for a much wider class of nonlinear systems than previously known, and prove the BQP-completeness of nonlinear oscillator problems of exponential size. In our analysis, we also obtain several results related to the Poincaré-Dulac theorem and diagonalization of the Carleman matrix, which could be of independent interest.

.
tldr: The paper extends quantum algorithms for nonlinear dynamics via Carleman embedding to broader stable, conservative, and non-resonant systems, and proves BQP-completeness for nonlinear oscillator problems.
motivation: Nonlinear dynamics are classically hard to simulate, and prior quantum algorithms based on Carleman embedding were limited to purely dissipative systems, excluding many important applications.
method: The authors correct prior technical analyses and derive convergence criteria using quadratic Lyapunov functions, conserved polynomial quantities, and non-resonant conditions for the Carleman scheme.
result: They show efficient quantum algorithms for a much wider class of nonlinear systems and establish BQP-completeness of exponential-size nonlinear oscillator problems, with additional results on the Poincaré-Dulac theorem and Carleman matrix diagonalization.
conclusion: The work significantly broadens the scope of quantum-simulable nonlinear dynamics but is primarily a quantum algorithms and complexity contribution, not directly aligned with the researcher's core quantum information or thermodynamics interests.

title: Floquet-ADAPT-VQE: A Quantum Algorithm To Simulate Non-Equilibrium Physics In Periodically Driven Systems
authors: Abhishek Kumar, Karunya Shirali, Nicholas J. Mayhall, Sophia E. Economou, And Edwin Barnes
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2247 (2026).

Periodically driven quantum systems exhibit many fascinating phenomena absent in equilibrium systems, but their simulation is more challenging than that of static systems. Consequently, quantum simulation of these systems offers greater opportunity for achieving quantum advantage. To build the foundation for simulating time-periodic Hamiltonians, we utilize the Floquet-Hilbert space formalism to transform the Hamiltonian into a time-independent form and provide its Pauli decomposition. Within this formalism, we develop a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm, Floquet-ADAPT-VQE, that produces three key quantities that govern periodically driven quantum dynamics: the quasienergy, the associated Floquet eigenstates, and expectation values of observables with respect to these eigenstates. The latter is achieved by applying a fixed-depth quantum circuit to an initial Floquet eigenstate—an efficient construction made possible by the Floquet-Hilbert space formalism. We also identify a suitable auxiliary initial state whose squared Floquet energy is independent of the number of auxiliary qubits as well as the driving frequency, which leads to better convergence with fewer ADAPT iterations. We demonstrate our algorithm by performing numerical simulations on a periodically driven XYZ model with a magnetic field. We also explore potential applications of our algorithm for studying various non-equilibrium phenomena in periodically driven systems.

.
tldr: The paper introduces Floquet-ADAPT-VQE, a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for simulating periodically driven quantum systems via the Floquet-Hilbert space formalism.
motivation: Periodically driven quantum systems exhibit rich non-equilibrium phenomena but are harder to simulate than static systems, motivating specialized quantum algorithms that could enable quantum advantage.
method: The authors transform a time-periodic Hamiltonian into a time-independent form using Floquet-Hilbert space, provide its Pauli decomposition, and develop an ADAPT-VQE-based algorithm with an auxiliary initial state to compute quasienergies, Floquet eigenstates, and observables.
result: They demonstrate the algorithm numerically on a periodically driven XYZ model with a magnetic field and show improved convergence with fewer ADAPT iterations using the auxiliary initial state.
conclusion: Floquet-ADAPT-VQE provides a promising route for studying non-equilibrium phenomena in periodically driven systems, though it is primarily a quantum simulation algorithm rather than a thermodynamic or information-theoretic result.

title: Limits To Black-box Amplification In Qma
authors: Scott Aaronson, Phillip Harris, And Freek Witteveen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2227 (2026).

We study the limitations of black-box amplification in the quantum complexity class [MATH]. Amplification is known to boost any inverse-polynomial gap between completeness and soundness to exponentially small error, and a recent result (Jeffery and Witteveen, 2025) shows that completeness can in fact be amplified to be doubly exponentially close to 1. We prove that this is optimal for black-box procedures: we provide a quantum oracle relative to which no [MATH] verification procedure using polynomial resources can achieve completeness closer to 1 than doubly exponential, or a soundness which is super-exponentially small. This is proven by making the oracle separation from (Aaronson, 2009) between [MATH] and [MATH] quantitative, using techniques from complex approximation theory.

.
tldr: The paper proves optimal limits on black-box amplification in QMA using a quantum oracle and complex approximation techniques.
motivation: Amplification is a fundamental primitive in quantum complexity, and recent work showed completeness in QMA can be amplified doubly exponentially; this paper asks whether that is the best possible for black-box procedures.
method: The authors construct a quantum oracle relative to which no polynomial-resource QMA verification procedure can achieve completeness closer to 1 than doubly exponential or soundness super-exponentially small, making a previous oracle separation quantitative via complex approximation theory.
result: They establish that doubly exponential completeness amplification is optimal for black-box QMA procedures, and that super-exponentially small soundness is impossible relative to their oracle.
conclusion: The work delineates fundamental black-box limitations of error reduction in QMA and provides a quantitative oracle separation with tools from approximation theory.

title: GPU-Accelerated Quantum Simulation Of Stabilizer Circuits
authors: Muhammad Osama, Dimitrios Thanos, And Alfons Laarman
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2225 (2026).

We introduce new parallel algorithms for efficiently simulating stabilizer (Clifford) circuits on GPUs, with a focus on data-parallel tableau evolution and scalable handling of projective measurements.
